newsitem.title: USA: Japan Big Bang 'do-or-die' project - FinMin official.
newsitem.headline: Japan Big Bang 'do-or-die' project - FinMin official.

text.p: Japan must move swiftly to reform its over-regulated financial markets or risk falling behind in the face of increasingly tough competition from abroad, a Japanese finance ministry official said on Thursday.

"Japan is now well behind compared to two other major markets, New York and London," Tadashi Iwashita, a ministry official attached to the Japanese embassy in Washington, told a luncheon organised by the National Economists Club.
"Unless we do something about that, we will be behind (along) with emerging markets. It's a do-or-die situation," he added.

After transaction values on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) increased dramatically in the late 1980s, they have declined sharply at the start of the 1990s and are now far below those measured on the New York or London bourses.

Iwashita said it was now clear that the increase in transaction values a decade ago had been "a complete bubble." The decline in the TSE's overall market share had been caused by overregulation that stifled innovation as much as the high cost of doing business in Japan, he added.

Tokyo's "Big Bang," first announced by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto late last year, envisages among other measures the lifting of sanctions on securities derivatives, liberalization of stock commissions, more stringent disclosure laws and scrapping a ban on financial holding companies.

The program, modelled on London's 1986 "Big Bang", is expected to force a major shake-out in Japan's financial sector, but experts have voiced doubts whether the nation's staid financial institutions have what it takes to become truly global players.
"The administration has made a considerable commitment. The rest is up to the players in the markets in Japan and the world," Iwashati said.
The ministry official held out the prospect of beneficial effects on other sectors of the economy and higher growth overall should the ambitious reform project succeed.

"If the Tokyo Big Bang will be a success, then this is an important case for deregulation in other areas," he said. "In the long run, I have no doubt it will have a very good impact on the economy overall."
